sources.title: Standard deviations and standard errors
sources.version: BMJ 2005;331(7521):903, Statistics Notes series; full text as archived in PubMed Central, retrieved 2026-07-25. DOI 10.1136/bmj.331.7521.903, PMID 16223828, PMCID PMC1255808
sources.locator: Whole article: the contrast between the standard deviation as a measure of variability and the standard error as the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean; the relation SE = SD divided by the square root of the sample size; the behaviour of each as the sample grows; and the closing passage on unlabelled plus-or-minus notation
sources.license: Copyright 2005, BMJ Publishing Group Ltd; free full text made available through PubMed Central. No open reuse licence is stated, so this pack uses the article for facts only.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts it states: that the standard deviation measures variability among individuals while the standard error measures the uncertainty around an estimated mean; that the sample mean varies from sample to sample and that variation is described by the sampling distribution of the mean, whose standard deviation is the standard error; that SE equals SD divided by the square root of the sample size; that the standard error falls as the sample size increases while the standard deviation does not tend to change; that about 95% of individuals lie within two standard deviations of the mean for normally distributed data and that about 95% of observations of any distribution usually fall within those limits; that the sampling-distribution principle extends to proportions, regression coefficients, and contrasts such as a difference between two means; and that a review of 88 articles published in 2002 found 12 (14%) failed to identify which measure of dispersion was reported, after which the BMJ adopted a policy of removing plus-or-minus signs and asking authors to state which quantity is quoted. No sentence, table, figure, or example from the article is reproduced or adapted. The cohort, every worked figure, all four scenes that rest on these facts, and all wording in this lesson are original.

sources.locator: Section 1.3.6.6.1, Normal Distribution, under the heading 'Theroretical Justification - Central Limit Theorem'
sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the three facts the page states about the central limit theorem as the sample size becomes large: that the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal regardless of the distribution of the original variable, that it is centred at the population mean of that variable, and that its standard deviation approaches the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. No wording, table, figure, or example from the handbook is reproduced or adapted; the theorem statement in the lesson was rewritten and every illustration around it is original. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

sources.title: Central limit theorem: the cornerstone of modern statistics
sources.version: Korean Journal of Anesthesiology 2017;70(2):144-156; full text as archived in PubMed Central, retrieved 2026-07-25. DOI 10.4097/kjae.2017.70.2.144, PMID 28367284, PMCID PMC5370305
sources.locator: Sections on the sampling distributions of small populations and the statement of the central limit theorem, and the discussion of the sample size at which the Student's t distribution is treated as equalling the normal distribution
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License (CC BY-NC 4.0), as stated on the article page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that a skewed population distribution does not prevent the distribution of sample means from approaching normality as the sample size increases; that the central limit theorem holds that the means of sufficiently large random samples are distributed normally with the population mean and a variance of the population variance divided by the sample size, regardless of the population distribution; that the sample means gather more closely around the population mean as the sample size grows; and that a sample size of about 30 is the conventional point at which the Student's t distribution is treated as equalling the normal distribution. No wording, table, figure, worked demonstration, or example from the article is reproduced or adapted, and the article's non-commercial licence condition is not relied on because nothing from it is reused. The pharmacy example and every other illustration in this lesson are original.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the reference values it states for the fasting plasma glucose test, namely 99 mg/dL or below as normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL as prediabetes and 126 mg/dL or above as diabetes, for the statement that a doctor will usually use a second test to confirm a diabetes diagnosis, and for the definition of fasting as having nothing to eat or drink except sips of water. These values appear in this lesson only to give the audit-planning case a real width to measure an estimate's precision against. The clinic, the two proposals, and all wording are original, and the lesson makes no diagnostic, monitoring, or treatment recommendation.
